utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd-like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the -- a long time ago, at the beginning of your testimony and which you have repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you haven't repeated it but I've reminded you. Let's be precise. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask to have our transcript from yesterday, if it's possible to have in e-court, because I think I have to make one correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have page and line numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. It's page 36651, lines 12 and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not easy to get it on our screen, Mr. Lukic, but we could just perhaps read. And you said 36651.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that can assist, Ms. Janet can do it on Sanction, can bring up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's possible, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's there. If I'm not -- no. There we are. 36651. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I will read from yesterday's transcript what is entered as a question, and it is recorded that I asked you: "Is it correct that, as a scientist, you cannot exclude the possibility that any or some of these people were killed in combat?" I would like that ask you today, actually, is it correct that, as a scientist, you cannot exclude the possibility that none of these people were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that equally applies. I'm not entirely sure what the definition of "combat" is, but if I said it about some, it would equally apply for them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to have now on our screens P7443, MFI. And we need page 7 in English, paragraph 3, and page 8 in B/C/S, also paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll continue in B/C/S, Doctor. [Interpretation] Doctor, yesterday at one point in time, you told us that as far as boots were concerned, the victims were not wearing any. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall ever saying that. It's not what I've said in my report either. I've said that the bulk of these individuals had -- were wearing ordinary shoes. A few of them did have boots, but that's different to what you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 16, line 11 of the transcript said that. That is what was entered. So I just wanted to clarify the matter. So I accept what you're saying now. That is what I find in your report, precisely what you said just now. So, in the report it says that 15 per cent -- or, rather, 26 persons wore boots. Is that right? We see that in paragraph 3 on page 8.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've recorded that 26 individuals -- of those that had footwear, of those that had footwear had boots of some sort, although boots extends from a Wellington boot to a kind of fairly heavy training boot, a sort of -- it's difficult to describe. But a sort of a heavier shoe than, say, a training shoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to dwell on this part of your report briefly, the one that has to do with clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you certain that the B/C/S version is the right one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was watching English. Yeah, we need page 8 in B/C/S as well, and we need to go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you sure that it's really page 8? Because we have page 8 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems that there are several versions of this document uploaded. We need the next page in -- anyway. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I would just like to ask you something briefly. Is it correct that you did not deal with the following question, whether any of the Muslim forces in 1992 wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that at -- whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what is not in the report, at least for this Chamber, is not dealt with by the witness. Whatever he may have done and not written down in his report, we do not know, but if the witness did not express himself on that, then, for us, he has not delegate with it. If you have a reason to believe that he did deal with some matters, of course, you can ask him, but let's avoid that we have to ask the witness all the things he did not deal with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, there were [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. -- unless there's something which -- not a debate, but if there's something unfair in what I said, please address me; if not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, were there any examples in your practice - you did work on Srebrenica after all - were combatants buried with weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anybody being buried with a weapon, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the information that you gathered and that you spoke of in the beginning of your report, did you deal with combat between the Serb and Muslim forces in the area of Prijedor at that time, especially in the area of Brdo? And have you heard of the Kurevo forest?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no specific information about Muslim forces at that time. I may have -- I think I've heard of the word "Kurevo forest," but I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what you were asked in Mr. Karadzic's trial: "Did you know that there was a legal requirement to sanitize the area?" In Mr. Karadzic's transcript, that is page 22708, lines 15 to 21. You said that you were not aware of that legal requirement. Afterwards, did you deal with that requirement, namely, to sanitize the area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by deal with that requirement. Did I consider it or research it or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we get -- sanitize which area?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's legal obligation for any area after the combat operations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Now which area are you talking about that the witness is supposed to have considered?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Brdo area in Prijedor municipality where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the answer is I did not make any further detailed inquiry of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Doctor. [Interpretation] We'll stay on the same page. We need the paragraph at the bottom of the page, below the photograph. You said the following: "In terms of personal possession, many of the men - 83, rather, 28 per cent - were carrying identification cards." Then you say 45 of the men had watches, 44 had money "and smaller numbers had wallets and jewellery." In your view, is that characteristic of a situation when people were not searched?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- certainly in terms of identification documents, this was a site that we saw them more often than previous circumstances -- previous occasions. So it was quite a regular feature to see the ID documents. In terms of perhaps watches, cigarettes, et cetera, they were frequently found in other sites as well, but certainly ID documents were -- seemed to be a quite an unusual number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean higher or lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A higher number, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the course of your work, did you come upon the obligation of the forces that take a certain area to search individuals there and take away certain possessions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need page 8 in the English version; 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are referring to numbers of gun-shot injuries. At the very outset, you say that gun-shot injuries were found in all but ten cases.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you have any idea as to how these other people had lost their lives, namely, those who had not sustained gun-shot injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are dealt with at the end of the report with the unascertained cases. Some of these cases at least had no obvious gun-shot injuries in the parts of the bodies which were still present, but some of them had major parts missing, perhaps the head or a leg, in which there could well have been gun-shot injuries. So that could account for some of them. One or two of them were complete bodies and we could not find any gun-shot injury. They may have died in some other way, not related to gun-shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, details to be found on page 15, bottom part. 13 no convincing cause of death could be found. That's where the answers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But still I want to ask if doctor can exclude natural cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you can't exclude. And it says here clearly: There's possible gun-shot injury of the face, 051T. That means as long as that is not ascertained, this witness, as he clearly says, couldn't tell us how that person died and that includes natural causes of death. Because if you don't know, you can't exclude anything. I mean, that's so logic. Let's not spend time on the things that are obvious, that are clearly -- perhaps not literally, but common sense, normal reasoning brings to us these answers and that is true for many of the questions you have put to the witness. You may now proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "many," Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Many -- do I have to give a number, Mr. Lukic. I said you could proceed. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in this trial we can lean on common sense, we don't have to have evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We need to have evidence but we should not -- when you're talking about excluding, you should not exclude common sense; that is, normal reasoning, logical reasoning. And if the witness has for 13 persons given exact details of why they couldn't ascertain the cause of death, then, of course, it's not of any use to ask whether it could have been natural causes. Because that is simple logic. And the witness referred to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would remind Your Honour again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Mr. Lukic, we now move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, in this part that starts with estimated number of injuries -- [In English] assessing numbers of injuries, yes, thank you, this is what you say. For example --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a specific reference as to where Mr. Lukic is reading from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you give an indication where you are reading from? The interpreters can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's number of gun-shot injuries. It's part after the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, line 4: "Where there is a clear single shot to the head with no injury anywhere else, then the number of shots can be stated with some confidence. But, where, for instance, there are shots passing through the trunk, where damage to more than one area could represent the track of a single bullet travelling in a certain direction, or instead could be two or more separate shots to different areas, then numbers are less sure." So, Doctor, that number, 710 -- no, 709, sorry, 709 injuries that you found, could it be changed in view of this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be higher. I don't think it would be lower because we've -- I'm working on a minimum number. Yes, it could certainly be higher, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, you say in the same paragraph, in line 7 there's a sentence that starts with the word "equally." This is what you say: "When considering gun-shot injuries to the arms when there are also injuries to the trunk or even the head, consideration would have to be given to these all being part of the same track." Would you agree, Doctor, that this could also be a separate injury, that is to say, caused by a different bullet or a different shrapnel, and that that could also increase the number of 709?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intervene again. The witness has explained this in detail. He has explained yesterday exactly that -- what traces he found. He has even explained as to the position from where to where the bullet trajectory in the body would lead him to say, Well, it could be two, but let's keep on the safe side and let's take it one. Only where this witness was convinced that these were two separate bullets, that the witness counted them as two. It is fully explained, it's repetitious, unless, Witness, you consider the question to be anything else. If not, Mr. Lukic will put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you worked on different calculations here and we're going to get to that right now. On this page, we have the first table that is at the bottom of the page, and that is Table 3. Would you agree, then, that all of these figures stated here are relative, that they were not stated with full certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent that's true. I think they are reasonably accurate. I quite agree that if we have underestimated injuries, some of the -- some of these figures would rise. It's -- I think it's a fairly reasonably accurate assumption, though, or analysis. I think particularly with the single shots. I think that has to be an accurate number. And particularly -- really confusion comes or the difficulty comes if -- of injuries below the head. Where there's injuries to the head it's usually very clear to say it's one shot or at most two shots. So the single gun-shot injuries, I think that's an accurate figure. The -- whether it's two, three, for the trunk is -- yes, it's a little less certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, could it be lower or higher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose conceivably they could be very slightly lower. I think only a matter of one or two. There may be occasions in which I have worked out or to my satisfaction that there are two injuries. In fact it was one. But really only a very small number. And I kind of bent over backwards to try and associate injuries, so I'd -- I think, if anything, the number will go up rather than down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us if these mathematical comparisons form part of your regular tasks as pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a regular pathologist, one is dealing with just a single -- a single case, usually a fresh body. Gun-shot injuries are much easier to assess in these situations. This is a completely different context. I try and apply similar principles but I have to make allowances for the fact that these are not fresh bodies and they're distorted, et cetera. So estimating in individuals from a mass grave is a completely different context from a routine case in a fresh body in a mortuary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for my understanding, what did you exactly refer to when you said "mathematical comparisons"? What kind of comparisons did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have in mind Table 3, Table 4, Figure 3, Table 5. JUDE ORIE: Yes. That's -- I don't see the comparison. What I see is numbers, at least in 3, but I'll have a look at 4, 5, or 6, whether there were any comparisons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is even one comparison in Table 5 with other grave-sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did you receive that task from someone else or did you do this of your own initiative, to produce these comparisons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was entirely my own initiative. As was the style of the report and the analysis was entirely my initiative. I just thought it would be a helpful way to analyse or portray the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will need the following page in both versions. Actually, I apologise. Let's stay with page 8 for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you discuss the distribution of gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that in Table 4 we have the list of 709 gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have Table 4 on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have it in a second, Your Honour. It's on the next page, so we have to start from this page, from the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then let's deal with this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we can see under item 2, distribution of the gun-shot injuries, you say the following: "In terms of what injuries were caused by these 709 bullets, Table 4 below lists them according to body region." Doctor, first of all, yesterday I asked you whether we were dealing with 709 bullets or wounds, injuries. You said that did you not count the bullets but the injuries themselves.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yet here we see this reference to 709 bullets. Was this simply misrecorded?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a different context. 709 gun-shot injuries must -- each one must have been caused by a bullet. So this reference here is to these projectiles which caused these 709 gun-shot injuries, that is not to say that I found 709 bullets but they had to be caused by a bullet. That was my interpretation that this was a gun-shot injury, nothing else could have caused it. So I think it's fair enough to imply that if there are 709 gun-shot injuries, there must have been 709 bullets to cause each one. Or one of 709 to cause each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard today that the figure was at least 709, possibly higher; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the next page in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a follow-up question. Mr. Clark, you have explained to us that sometimes by the -- something visible in -- well, let's say, the lower part of the body and in the head, that you sometimes concluded that it wasn't certain that there were two bullets and for that reason you counted those two markings on the body for one injury, one bullet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if, well, let's say, you find something on the chest and on the head, how did you categorise them as body region, head or trunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By recollection, it would be the first part of the body which was struck. So if it had gone through the head and then ended up in the chest, I would count that as a gun-shot injury to the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were always sufficiently able to see where the bullet would have entered and where it would have left other marks so as to be sufficiently certain that you could qualify the injury as inflicted on the head or the chest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may be the occasional case in which I got the direction wrong but this was my best -- best estimate of the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And if you compare them then later in Table 5, did you make similar assessments for the other sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and this is where it is valid to -- because we do have a similar population, if you like, similar situations of mass graves, and I think it's -- this is a reasonable place to compare these, and the figures are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same difficulties in interpretation occurred in each of these other grave-sites and my same -- I adopted the same approach to the analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand you well, you allow for minor -- minor mistakes here, but overall, you are confident that you were sufficiently able to establish where the bullet entered the body so as to qualify the injury as you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I did spend a lot of time looking at these, the reports, the photographs, and -- so it's not just a quick analysis. There is -- this is actually quite detailed thought behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you provide the distribution of injuries on the victims found in the Tomasica mass grave. You say you compared to some other mass graves. Did you compare it in terms of number of injuries that would be customary for combat? Did you ever refer or write about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Presumably you're talking about combat situations elsewhere in the world or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anywhere. I have not specifically compared that. I have to say these figures for combat situations elsewhere are sometimes quite difficult to get hold of. But, yes, I have not compared them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that it was surprising to find so many injuries to the head and neck. Yesterday, Judge Orie asked you what position you had in mind, whether it was the standing position that you considered, and I wanted to ask you today if you would agree that the distribution of injuries is different, depending on whether the person is standing, kneeling, or lying down?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I've used the word "random" here and I'm envisaging a standard situation of a person standing upright, and that is the -- if that is the case, then it seems to me that the head -- there was an excess number of shots to the head. Entirely correct, you could -- it depends entirely on the position of the body. If only the head is exposed, then naturally there would be a preponderance of injuries to the head. So I'm happy to consider any scenario, but this is based on a a kind of random standard situation of somebody who is upright.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just clarification on an earlier question, Dr. Clark. You were asked at page 16, line 5, you know -- you said you were being asked about situations elsewhere in the world, combat figures, and whether you consider these combat figures in other situations. How would a comparison of your -- of combat figures in -- figures in combat assist you as a pathologist in the work you were doing like the work for purposes of determining the cause of death in the Tomasica issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would show to me that perhaps in genuine combat situations, most gun-shot injuries, most soldiers sustain injuries to the head or to the trunk. That may be the position. I don't know. I don't have these figures. What I do know, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But would that be part of your brief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be part of my interest rather than -- rather than brief. I do know, however, that in a combat situation, the injury that predominates in soldiers are explosive injuries, so shrapnel injuries, rather than gun-shots. More soldiers will die from explosive injuries than gun-shot injuries. That I do know. That has been well established and repeated. But I don't have figures for the specific parts of the body which are most commonly damaged. And, of course, combat situations will vary themselves anyway, from people who are on the ground or kneeling or standing upright, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the distribution of injuries that you have shown here on the body; so Figure 3. We see that in some cases, you mention as the cause of death the injuries to the lower extremities; gun-shot injuries, that is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not very many but ... maybe four cases, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, there was only a small number of such injuries to the legs; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whether fatal [Realtime transcript read in error "facial"] or otherwise, a small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could this indication that such a small number of legs -- injuries to the legs tell you anything about the position those people were in, that they may have perhaps been lying down?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely possible that the legs were, in some way, covered or protected either from kneeling or lying down. Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, I read as one of your answers. The question being: "In any case, there was only a small number of such injuries to the legs; correct? Your answer was: "Yes, whether facial or otherwise ..." I may not fully understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant -- I meant fatal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fatal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fatal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the table at the bottom of the page in English and it is on the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you compare different locations. The locations being Tomasica, Kozluk, Ravnice, Slap, and Knin, in Croatia. The table is titled: "Comparison of gun-shot injury distribution amongst different grave-sites." In this table, what is it that you are trying to indicate? For example, let's take Kozluk in Srebrenica. When you say distribution of gun-shot injuries, head and neck, in Tomasica it was 35 and in Kozluk, 23 per cent, does it mean that there were fewer executions in Kozluk than in Tomasica or more? What is the point of this comparison?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that the three pathologists who were in this mortuary felt there was an unusual number of cases that we were seeing with a gun-shot wound particularly to the back of the head. So I mean, that was natural observation. I thought it would be useful to try and quantify that and say were we justified in thinking that by comparing it with other grave-sites. So that's all I have done, and it does justify that to some extent. It does say that, yes, in this particular grave-site, the injuries to the head were more common than we saw in other sites. That's about as much as I would go. It's just simply a comparison to highlight the fact it was a recurring feature of the Tomasica cases to find a gun-shot injury to the head and particularly to the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that was explained in detail yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I needed it for the next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think we all remember it, but then put your next question to the witness. And let me already indicate now that this witness, I think where he established facts and made comparisons based on his experience, that he -- unless I misunderstood you, Mr. Clark, you refrained from explaining why this would have been the case and what conclusions you could draw from that because your expertise does not allow to do that, and it would be others, including a court, which finally would have to consider whether or not any conclusions can be drawn from it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's entirely correct. That's my approach to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic, with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think there is no need now since the -- you said that there is no -- I want -- my next question was whether the doctor had drawn any conclusions based on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has not, as he explained several times and as what I said earlier, if he would have drawn any relevant conclusions, we would have found them in the report. And I think that the witness, as he confirmed a minute ago, stayed well within the realm of his expertise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Next we need page 11 in the English and 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we see the table referring to the site of impact of bullets, head and neck, to the back of, 45 per cent. In order to avoid confusion, and you also specify that it refers to 246 shots to the head and neck, so we see that 45 per cent of those went to the back. However, if we take into account the number of 709 injuries, by my calculation it amounts to 15.6 per cent with regard to the number of injuries caused on slightly less than 300 bodies found in Tomasica. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a reasonable -- I haven't actually worked it out, but that would fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. I see that it's approximately time for a break. Your -- first of all, Mr. Clark, we take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that, and you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, in view of how the cross-examination developed, you're encouraged to review whether you could shorten your cross-examination and focus on matters which are -- really need explanation, have not been explained yet and are relevant. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I drastically shortened my questions. I should finish in the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I've told the Trial Chamber, and we are supposed to finish within the next ten to 15 minutes. I started the day today trying to correct something. However, thanks to my imperfect English, I actually made a mistake, so now I will have to read something out to you yet again and ask you about it yet again. I do apologise for going back to the same topic for the third time. Now I'm going to ask in B/C/S so that can you get the right interpretation. Doctor, is it correct that you, as a scientist, cannot exclude the possibility of all of those people who were found in Tomasica were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, I cannot exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I do apologise for having gone back to this several times. Now I'm just going to ask you a few general questions about your work. Is it correct that pathologists use protocols in order to reach standardized reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a variety of standardized reports, and every pathologist will have their own style of report, but it's certainly common to all pathologists to -- the process of examining a body is to do it in different stages, starting from outside and then coming to conclusions. So it's standard in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct when -- that when the cause of death is formulated, different pathologists can reach different conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I think you're probably implying two things there. The cause of death can be agreed. Different pathologists will have different wordings of it, perhaps, will word it slightly differently. But you're also correct in saying that with given findings, different pathologists will interpret these findings perhaps slightly differently. Put more emphasis on one finding than another. That would only to -- be what's expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. People do not die of bone damage but, rather, tissue damage, heart, artery, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and it's something that I have always emphasised in my reports, that all we're looking at, all the evidence we have in most of these cases is the damage to the bone. But as a pathologist who has done many, many thousands of ordinary cases, shall we say, I know that what lies beside that bone and what that damage to the bone -- what other damage it will cause, and I think -- I'm allowed professionally to then judge what would have -- the significance of damage to a particular bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that anthropologists have a greater role to play in such cases, say the case of mass graves, as compared to your everyday work when you deal with persons who are recently deceased?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the anthropologist, their expertise, is in the examination of bones, assessing physical features of that person from the bone, and also in looking at the trauma of -- to the bone. What they lack, however, is the ability to translate that damage to the likely medical consequences, and that is very much the role of the pathologist. But I think the pathologists increasingly also have an increasingly expertise in interpreting bone injury as well. But only the medical people can really assess the significance of injuries which have occurred with what they'll do and likely survival and ability to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, I think that you may have missed the gist of the question, which I think was whether the role of the anthropologist in larger in this kind of situation, mass graves, et cetera, compared to someone who was stabbed in a bar or someone who was everyday pathologist's practice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so. In a case like that, a stabbing or natural death, the anthropologist would not be involved. The anthropologist's main involvement is in cases of mass graves, where the remains are largely quite often reduced to a skeleton, so they can examine the bones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And often unidentified, does that play a role as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they have a role to play in identification. Actually probably less nowadays than in the past with the onset of DNA identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is that what you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I seek clarification with respect to one of your answers. Perhaps it's just a slip of the tongue. Page 24, line 6, you are recorded as having said: "But I think the pathologists increasingly also have an increasingly expertise in interpreting," and then there is a word missing, "injury as well. But only the medical people can really assess the significance of injuries ..." Are you saying the pathologists increasingly have the ability and the expertise or the -- or the anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the pathologist. For instance, in this work in Tomasica, the main people looking at the bodies were the pathologists. And in many parts of the world, there are no anthropologists, as such, and the pathologist has to do that -- that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just follow up on this very sentence. You're talking about the pathologists on the one hand and medical people on the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm meaning the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The same people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pathologists are always medically trained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, Doctor, may I ask you to tell us the difference between a decomposed body and skeletonised remains.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent skeletonised remains is decomposed but it's reached the ultimate stage of it. Decomposition starts almost very shortly after death as the body tissues degenerate and the end point will be a skeleton. So anything in between effectively is decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that it is very difficult to establish cause of death on a decomposed body? So we're taking into account the bodies that were found in Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it's very difficult. It is more difficult because we -- as a pathologist, in fresh bodies we rely on blood and swelling and bruising, et cetera, to interpret that which are not present in decomposed bodies, even these well-preserved Tomasica ones. It is certainly more difficult but we can -- when, you know, we see bullet injuries, I think that's still a fairly certain cause of death. We can still see these injuries. But in terms of natural disease or poisoning, et cetera, yes, it becomes much more difficult in decomposed bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following question in this context. If the decomposition of the body would be such that you would be hesitant to draw conclusions because of that state of the body, would you always clearly state that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would give a cause of death as unascertained, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we have 1D5774 on our screens, please. 1D5774. I don't know if there could be a mistake. We should have transcript in front of us. 1D05774, yes. In e-court we need page 48. And it's page -- we're on the right page. It's number 7388, transcript page from Popovic trial. We need line 21 and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read in English, Doctor. The question was: "Is it fair that doing an autopsy as a pathologist, it's very difficult, nearly impossible, to assess the cause of death on a decomposed body?" And your answer was: "A. It's very difficult, yes." In the last line, the question was - and we'll need to go to the next page when I finish this line - so line 25, I quote: "Q. And is it also true that with a skeletonised body, it is virtually impossible to determine the cause of death? "A. That's fair, yes." [Interpretation] So, Doctor, do you stand by your last statement today as well; namely, that it is almost impossible to determine the cause of death on skeletonised remains?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the context is slightly different. I can only imagine that the question I was being asked, that from a theoretical point of view, if all you have is a skeleton or a very decomposed body, can you 100 per cent say, tell the cause of death. And in that situation, yes, from a bone I cannot -- even with the damage there, I cannot say 100 per cent that that is the cause of death because the other tissues are missing. That, I imagine, is the context that I gave these answers. I would still stand to what I said this morning, that in the totality of dealing with these cases that it becomes -- is difficult but not impossible if you allow us to interpret what damage to a bone will cause in a normal body. That's perhaps not very clear, but I think the context is slightly different in these two statements. Whatever I was -- I would stick to what I said to you this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in addition, Dr. Clark, I thought you said a few minutes ago that for a skeletonised body where the cause of death could have been through poisoning or natural causes, that would be impossible to determine. You would say that that is unascertained, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. So that would be the difference. But if it was through injury, you may be able to tell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you in this respect the following: If you have a fully skeletonised body but, for example, a clear hole in the -- in the head where you can see where a projectile had entered head, would you under those circumstances draw conclusions as to whether such an injury would have caused death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would strongly imply that the -- the cause of death there. In theory, because, as we've already agreed, people don't die of damage to the bone but to what's around about it, in theory I could say no, but I think you've got to make professional allowance for the context of the case and allow us to interpret a gun-shot injury to the skull in the particular context that person has died from a gun-shot injury to the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas theoretically you couldn't exclude that the person died from natural causes, then was dead and was shot with a bullet through the head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. And I've explored these arguments previously in my previous reports, et cetera, very fully. Again we come back to common sense as to what is likely, particularly with large numbers of people who have been shot. The reverse would be that these people have all died of natural causes or poisoning and then been all shot after death. Now is that a reasonable suggestion to put? So I think Your Honour has got it correct, that in pure pathological theory, from a bone I cannot say the cause of death, but I think we can think wider than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Doctor, for answering our questions. That was all we had for you at this moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark -- and I know that you've been addressed as Dr. Clark, and when I say "Mr. Clark" it has got nothing do with any depreciation of your authority, it's just my way of expressing myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. You've explained that before so, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, this concludes your testimony, but I hope that it really concludes your testimony and that we don't see you back in a couple of months. Not because it wouldn't be a pleasure but because we want to proceed with this case. Mr. Clark, I'd like to thank you very much for coming again and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties, were put to you by the Judges, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the usher could prepare the next witness to remain on standby, but meanwhile I will deliver a decision in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is a ... one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will now deliver its decision on expertise of Mile Poparic and Zorica Subotic with regard to their four reports on mortar attacks and small-arms fire in the Sarajevo area between 1992 and 1995 and the use of modified aircraft bombs in the Sarajevo area between 1994 and 1995. On the 13th of April of this year, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of four expert reports, co-authored by Poparic and Subotic, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution filed its notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis on the 13th of May, submitting that it does not challenge the expert status of Poparic and Subotic or the relevance of the "Report on Mortar Attacks on the Sarajevo Area - Incidents at the Markale Market," and of the majority of the remaining three reports. It requests the exclusion of portions of these three reports due to lack of relevance. To the extent that the reports are admitted, the Prosecution does not accept their conclusions and therefore wishes to cross-examine the witnesses. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October, 2012, decision concerning Richard Butler. On the basis of Poparic's and Subotic's curricula vitae, and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute their qualifications as a weapons and military equipment expert and a ballistics, fire-arms and cold weapons expert, respectively, the Chamber is satisfied that they have specialised knowledge and expertise, and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the evidence presented by the Prosecution during its case in-chief. With regard to the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the witnesses, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Poparic and Subotic to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine them. Based on the forgoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules, that the Defence may call Mile Poparic and Zorica Subotic to testify as expert witnesses and that they shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber also instructs the Defence to review the reports and respond to the Prosecution's submission that portions of the reports should be excluded because these portions relate to unscheduled or dropped incidents from the indictment, address areas outside the scope of the reports, and challenge the evidence of witnesses who did not provide evidence in this case, and do that within two weeks of the date of this decision. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of the expert reports to the time of the witnesses' testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was reminded by the Court's ruling just now that the Defence requested on the 30th of June to add 21 documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list for use with Witness Misic who will be coming up shortly, and I wanted to note for the benefit of the Bench and the parties that the Prosecution has no objection to this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record. And, Ms. Tabeau, you are suffering from administrative matters still to be dealt with. Ms. Tabeau, before you give evidence -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've made a solemn declaration already in this case. Therefore, there's no need to give that solemn declaration again. But I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by it, and the solemn declaration was that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you will first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli. You find her to your right, and you may know it already but Ms. D'Ascoli is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And good morning, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can I ask you to describe the folder that I see you have with you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: This is a folder containing a few documents that are related to my speaking today here in this courtroom. I have my report, Tomasica report, clean copy. I have the annexes to the report, clean copy again. I have the short notes I made in relation to the victims from Jakarina Kosa, again some tables related to Jakarina Kosa victims, a sample of the ICMP data based on which I made the analysis for Jakarina Kosa, and a short annex I prepared for these victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you always make clear to this Chamber when you're consulting any material which is not part of your report so that we know that you're using other sources as known to us at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may intervene. If I could just ask for some clarification. When she says "short notes," I don't know what that is and I don't see it on the list, so I don't know if that is a document I already have or if it's an additional document that I would be entitled to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- actually this short note, as I called it, is -- are a few pages, six pages, as far as I remember, consisting of actually only some statistics in some tables and no text whatsoever. And as far as I remember, I -- this note should have been disclosed to the Defence as part of my proofing notes. So there is no text, no research discussion, anything like that. Just a set of results of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, can you confirm that --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau is referring to document marked with 65 ter 32738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which has been --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Which has been disclosed to the Defence. Mr. Ivetic can confirm. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put just one additional question for clarification. The tables you are referring to contained in this note, are they are also contained in your report and the annexes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The notes and the annexes to the notes are not contained in my Tomasica report. It is separate and additional to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I will go into that later during the course of the examination. Can I please have 65 ter 31100 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You have been a demographer for more than 30 years; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you recently provide the OTP with an updated curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Once the document is on the screen, I would ask you whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: It is your updated CV?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your current profession is.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I am working at the ICTY in the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY as a demographer and a senior research officer. I am working on research into victims and victimisation patterns.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you were employed in the past as well in the Demographics Unit of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I started my employment with the OTP in September the year 2000 and recently had a break of two and a half years, after which I returned in March 2014 to resume the same responsibilities as I had before. In that break of two and a half years, I was coming to the ICTY each year, first to testify and prepare for the testimony in Karadzic, and, second time, to do the same for the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: The totals are correct, I made sure that they are.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this additional row provided is the penultimate one now on the tables.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.text: Therefore, does this document accurately reflect the corrections you wanted to make to your report and are you satisfied with its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: Yes. Just a second, and -- yes, can you confirm, is this the document containing the fours annexes that you produced together with your expert report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in respect of these four annexes, did you have an opportunity to review them before testifying?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I also reviewed the annexes.

utterances.text: And I understand you had some additional information to provide in respect of one of the annexes; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: Could I -- one second. The title reads: Reassociation, then the number 81, of the 46 cases split within the Tomasica grave. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the -- the capital has no meaning at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]

utterances.text: Your Honours, we have added this presentation to the list of exhibits for this witness and it is uploaded in e-court with 65 ter 32753. This presentation, these slides are explanatory in nature, demonstrative rather than evidentiary. However, I do plan to tender it into evidence to facilitate also the review of Ms. Tabeau's evidence, and therefore I would ask that also this document be marked for identification pending cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, 65 ter number 32753 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P7453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. I take it, Ms. D'Ascoli, that we don't need to have that one under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
